title: How To Avoid Losing Your Students’ Attention https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/11/10/how-to-avoid-losing-your-students-attention/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies a common teacher instinct—speeding up instruction when attention starts to wane—as a mistake that makes things worse. He walks through why: rushing causes teachers to skip the details that make lessons interesting, makes lessons harder to follow, triggers excitability, and signals to students that class is wrapping up so they mentally check out early. The article then offers the opposite prescription: when attention fades, slow down and add more detail rather than less. He illustrates this with an extended example of teaching students to place science samples in a ziplock bag, showing how granular, even trivial-seeming details (the history of the zipper, precise hand positioning) pull students deeper into a lesson. Rich, specific detail, he argues, is what makes students lose track of time and become fully absorbed in a lesson.
points: Speeding up instruction when student attention wanes is identified as a common but counterproductive teacher instinct.
Rushing makes lessons boring by causing teachers to skip the details that make content interesting and easier to follow.
Talking faster also triggers excitability, a major cause of misbehavior, and signals to students that it's time to mentally move on.
The recommended fix is the opposite of rushing: slow down and add more specific, granular detail when attention starts to fade.
A detailed classroom example (teaching students to bag science samples) shows how granular detail pulls students deeper into absorption in a lesson.
quotes: As attention starts to wane . . . Eyelids droop. Fingers tap. Bodies sigh. . . . the teacher will speed up their instruction.
But this is a big mistake—because it only makes things worse.
The urge to rush and get done quickly will inevitably cause you to gloss over details, which are the most important element in making your lessons interesting.
Talking faster is a sure recipe for excitability, which is one of the biggest causes of misbehavior.
Speeding up acts as a triggering mechanism. It signals to students that you’re wrapping it up, which causes them to move on mentally, and sometimes physically, to the next activity.
When you notice attention waning—or, better yet, to avoid ever losing your students’ attention—slow down and focus on details .
They’re compelling and fascinating and pull students so deep into the lesson that they forget where they are.
